lesson.title: Either One or the Other, Never Both: Disjoint Events
lesson.summary: Disjoint events, also called mutually exclusive events, share no outcomes at all, and knowing one happened actually guarantees the other did not, the opposite of independence.
lesson.body:
Two events are called disjoint, or equivalently mutually exclusive, when they share no outcomes at all, meaning it is impossible for both to happen on the same trial of the random phenomenon. Disjoint and mutually exclusive are simply two names mathematicians and statisticians both use for the exact same idea, so encountering either term in a textbook or on an exam should trigger the same picture: two events with completely empty overlap. This distinction matters because a great deal of later probability work depends on first checking, correctly, whether two events can possibly occur together at all before deciding how to combine their probabilities.

It helps to see a disjoint pair and a non disjoint pair side by side. Roll a single fair die and let A be the event the roll is even, {2, 4, 6}, and let B be the event the roll is odd, {1, 3, 5}. These two sets share no elements, so A and B are disjoint, which matches common sense since no single roll can be both even and odd. Now let C be the event the roll is prime, {2, 3, 5}. C is not disjoint from A, because the outcome 2 belongs to both, and C is not disjoint from B either, because 3 and 5 belong to both. A single roll of 2 makes both A and C happen simultaneously, which is exactly what disjoint events are defined to rule out.

A frequent point of confusion is mixing up disjoint with independent, but the two ideas are not just different, they actually pull in opposite directions. If two events are disjoint and both have a nonzero chance of happening, then learning that one of them occurred tells you with certainty that the other one did not, which is about as strong a dependence between two events as is possible. Independent events, covered in an upcoming chapter, are ones where learning that one happened tells you nothing at all about the other. Disjoint events with positive probability can never be independent, because knowing A happened collapses the probability of B all the way down to zero. This is one of the most common mix ups on probability exams, so it is worth remembering as a rule of thumb: disjoint events are strongly dependent, not independent.

Being disjoint has a direct payoff for computing probabilities: when two events cannot overlap, finding the probability that one or the other happens is just a matter of adding their individual probabilities together, with no risk of counting any outcome twice. Returning to the die example, P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(B) = 3/6 = 1/2, and since A and B are disjoint, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. That total of exactly 1 makes sense here because every possible roll is either even or odd, so A and B together account for the entire sample space with nothing left over and nothing double counted.

The next chapter takes this addition idea and generalizes it to handle events that are not disjoint, like the prime and even events above that do share an outcome. Simply adding their probabilities would double count that shared outcome, so the general addition rule builds in a correction for exactly that overlap.
